case_info.scenario: A 51-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of progressive memory loss and left limb numbness. She had been treated for cerebral infarction; however, the symptoms worsened. Medical history was unremarkable. She graduated from high school and worked as a driver. Smoking history and alcohol misuse were denied. One of her parents died in their late 60s with cognitive decline. On examination, her Mini-Mental State Examination score was 22, and her Montreal Cognitive Assessment score was 11. Cranial nerve tests revealed left-sided central facial palsy and lingual palsy. Pinprick sensation was decreased in the left arm. Results of other neurological or general examinations were unremarkable. The following investigations had normal or negative results: complete blood cell count, urine and stool analysis, liver and kidney function, cardiac enzymes, electrolytes, blood glucose, lipids, coagulation, homocysteine, vitamins, serum tumor markers, infectious panel, lupus panel, vasculitis antibodies (anti–neutrophil cytoplasmic and anti–neutrophil cytoplasmic), and demyelination antibodies (aquaporin 4 and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein). Seventy-two–hour electrocardiography detected no atrial fibrillation. Right-side heart contrast echocardiography found no right-to-left shunts on Valsalva maneuvers. Results of cerebrospinal fluid analysis were unremarkable. There were no oligoclonal bands. Enhanced cerebrospinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed diffuse subcortical white matter hyperintensities and corpus callosum atrophy. Diffusion-weighted imaging revealed multifocal restricted diffusion in the corpus callosum with corresponding low apparent diffusion coefficient values (Figure, A and B). Enhanced cerebrospinal MRI showed diffuse subcortical white matter hyperintensities and corpus callosum atrophy (Figure, C). Magnetic resonance angiography showed no atherosclerosis or stenosis.

options.C: Adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia

case_info.answer: Adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia
case_info.caption: Abnormal diffusion in the genu (A) and splenium (B) of the corpus callosum and bilateral diffuse subcortical white matter hyperintensities (C).
case_info.explanation: C. Adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia Progressive cognitive impairment, leukoencephalopathy, and corpus callosum abnormalities are the key features of the case. The restricted diffusion in corpus callosum has a radiologic differential, including acute infarction, acute demyelination, and hypercellularity, but it can also be seen, more rarely, in hereditary disorders. Perforating arteries branching from the carotid and vertebrobasilar system supply the genu and splenium of corpus callosum, respectively. Cardiac embolism (choice A) can cause multifocal abnormal diffusion in the corpus callosum by affecting both artery systems. However, this patient had no risk factors, such as atrial fibrillation or patent foramen ovale. Isolated corpus callosum infarction is also rare due to its rich blood supply. Autoimmune diseases, such as systemic lupus erythematosus, multiple sclerosis, and neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, can cause demyelination in the corpus callosum. However, the normal spinal MRI results, negative antibody results, and absence of oligoclonal bands (for multiple sclerosis) make these diagnoses unlikely. Another condition is Susac syndrome (choice B), which can cause abnormal diffusion in the splenium of the corpus callosum, known as the snowball sign. However, the absence of retinopathy and hearing loss argue against this disorder. Marchiafava-Bignami disease (choice D) is a rare cause of demyelination that mainly affects corpus callosum. It is caused by long-term alcoholism and is characterized by symptoms such as dementia, seizures, and ataxia. The absence of alcoholism and normal B vitamin levels make this a less likely choice. The time course of progression, diffuse white matter hyperintensities, corpus callosum abnormalities, and family history led to the consideration of hereditary leukoencephalopathies, such as metachromatic leukodystrophy, adrenoleukodystrophy, cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts, and leukoencephalopathy, retinal vasculopathy with cerebral leukocencephalopathy, and systemic manifestations, Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, and adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia (ALSP; choice C). Therefore, a gene test is warranted (choice B). We performed whole-exome genome sequencing and found a likely pathogenic variant (c.1969+1G>A) in the patient’sCSF1Rgene, supporting the diagnosis of ALSP. ALSP is a neurodegenerative disorder caused by variations in theCSF1Rgene. The encoded CSF1R protein is a transmembrane tyrosine kinase receptor expressed dominantly in mononuclear phagocytic cells and microglia. Mutant CSF1R leads to white matter demyelination, axonal spheroids, and pigmented macrophages neuropathologically. More than 70 variations, including missense, nonsense, and frameshift variations, have been associated with ALSP, classified as primary microgliopathy. Like other leukoencephalopathies, the clinical picture of ALSP is highly heterogeneous and nonspecific. Symptoms typically appear between the ages of 30 and 60 years, including cognitive impairment (eg, memory loss, difficulty with language, changes in behavior and personality), muscle weakness, tremors, parkinsonism, and seizures. ALSP is often misdiagnosed as multiple sclerosis, stroke, or other neurodegenerative disorders, such as parkinsonism or frontal-temporal dementia. Neuroimaging provides important diagnostic clues. Radiological features may include bilaterally diffuse white matter hyperintensities, brain calcifications, multifocal abnormal diffusion, cortical atrophy, and thinning of the corpus callosum. U fibers, cerebellar dentate, and peduncles are usually spared. Notably, unlike multiple sclerosis or ischemic infarction, the abnormal diffusion foci are persistent for several months or more.1The present case highlights the utility of atrophic corpus callosum with persistent abnormal diffusion as a specific neuroimaging marker for ALSP.2 Currently, symptomatic treatment is the mainstay option. Studies with small sample sizes have proposed hematopoietic stem cell transplant as a potential disease-modifying therapy.3However, more clinical trials are needed to validate its long-term safety and efficacy. The patient declined hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, and she was clinically stable over a 3-month follow-up period.

Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 0.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.

       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.

[Clinical case]
A 51-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of progressive memory loss and left limb numbness. She had been treated for cerebral infarction; however, the symptoms worsened. Medical history was unremarkable. She graduated from high school and worked as a driver. Smoking history and alcohol misuse were denied. One of her parents died in their late 60s with cognitive decline. On examination, her Mini-Mental State Examination score was 22, and her Montreal Cognitive Assessment score was 11. Cranial nerve tests revealed left-sided central facial palsy and lingual palsy. Pinprick sensation was decreased in the left arm. Results of other neurological or general examinations were unremarkable. The following investigations had normal or negative results: complete blood cell count, urine and stool analysis, liver and kidney function, cardiac enzymes, electrolytes, blood glucose, lipids, coagulation, homocysteine, vitamins, serum tumor markers, infectious panel, lupus panel, vasculitis antibodies (anti–neutrophil cytoplasmic and anti–neutrophil cytoplasmic), and demyelination antibodies (aquaporin 4 and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein). Seventy-two–hour electrocardiography detected no atrial fibrillation. Right-side heart contrast echocardiography found no right-to-left shunts on Valsalva maneuvers. Results of cerebrospinal fluid analysis were unremarkable. There were no oligoclonal bands. Enhanced cerebrospinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed diffuse subcortical white matter hyperintensities and corpus callosum atrophy. Diffusion-weighted imaging revealed multifocal restricted diffusion in the corpus callosum with corresponding low apparent diffusion coefficient values (Figure, A and B). Enhanced cerebrospinal MRI showed diffuse subcortical white matter hyperintensities and corpus callosum atrophy (Figure, C). Magnetic resonance angiography showed no atherosclerosis or stenosis.

case_info.answer: Adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia
case_info.caption: Abnormal diffusion in the genu (A) and splenium (B) of the corpus callosum and bilateral diffuse subcortical white matter hyperintensities (C).
case_info.explanation: C. Adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia Progressive cognitive impairment, leukoencephalopathy, and corpus callosum abnormalities are the key features of the case. The restricted diffusion in corpus callosum has a radiologic differential, including acute infarction, acute demyelination, and hypercellularity, but it can also be seen, more rarely, in hereditary disorders. Perforating arteries branching from the carotid and vertebrobasilar system supply the genu and splenium of corpus callosum, respectively. Cardiac embolism (choice A) can cause multifocal abnormal diffusion in the corpus callosum by affecting both artery systems. However, this patient had no risk factors, such as atrial fibrillation or patent foramen ovale. Isolated corpus callosum infarction is also rare due to its rich blood supply. Autoimmune diseases, such as systemic lupus erythematosus, multiple sclerosis, and neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, can cause demyelination in the corpus callosum. However, the normal spinal MRI results, negative antibody results, and absence of oligoclonal bands (for multiple sclerosis) make these diagnoses unlikely. Another condition is Susac syndrome (choice B), which can cause abnormal diffusion in the splenium of the corpus callosum, known as the snowball sign. However, the absence of retinopathy and hearing loss argue against this disorder. Marchiafava-Bignami disease (choice D) is a rare cause of demyelination that mainly affects corpus callosum. It is caused by long-term alcoholism and is characterized by symptoms such as dementia, seizures, and ataxia. The absence of alcoholism and normal B vitamin levels make this a less likely choice. The time course of progression, diffuse white matter hyperintensities, corpus callosum abnormalities, and family history led to the consideration of hereditary leukoencephalopathies, such as metachromatic leukodystrophy, adrenoleukodystrophy, cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts, and leukoencephalopathy, retinal vasculopathy with cerebral leukocencephalopathy, and systemic manifestations, Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, and adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia (ALSP; choice C). Therefore, a gene test is warranted (choice B). We performed whole-exome genome sequencing and found a likely pathogenic variant (c.1969+1G>A) in the patient’sCSF1Rgene, supporting the diagnosis of ALSP. ALSP is a neurodegenerative disorder caused by variations in theCSF1Rgene. The encoded CSF1R protein is a transmembrane tyrosine kinase receptor expressed dominantly in mononuclear phagocytic cells and microglia. Mutant CSF1R leads to white matter demyelination, axonal spheroids, and pigmented macrophages neuropathologically. More than 70 variations, including missense, nonsense, and frameshift variations, have been associated with ALSP, classified as primary microgliopathy. Like other leukoencephalopathies, the clinical picture of ALSP is highly heterogeneous and nonspecific. Symptoms typically appear between the ages of 30 and 60 years, including cognitive impairment (eg, memory loss, difficulty with language, changes in behavior and personality), muscle weakness, tremors, parkinsonism, and seizures. ALSP is often misdiagnosed as multiple sclerosis, stroke, or other neurodegenerative disorders, such as parkinsonism or frontal-temporal dementia. Neuroimaging provides important diagnostic clues. Radiological features may include bilaterally diffuse white matter hyperintensities, brain calcifications, multifocal abnormal diffusion, cortical atrophy, and thinning of the corpus callosum. U fibers, cerebellar dentate, and peduncles are usually spared. Notably, unlike multiple sclerosis or ischemic infarction, the abnormal diffusion foci are persistent for several months or more.1The present case highlights the utility of atrophic corpus callosum with persistent abnormal diffusion as a specific neuroimaging marker for ALSP.2 Currently, symptomatic treatment is the mainstay option. Studies with small sample sizes have proposed hematopoietic stem cell transplant as a potential disease-modifying therapy.3However, more clinical trials are needed to validate its long-term safety and efficacy. The patient declined hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, and she was clinically stable over a 3-month follow-up period.

* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be

   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

case_info.answer: Adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia
case_info.caption: Abnormal diffusion in the genu (A) and splenium (B) of the corpus callosum and bilateral diffuse subcortical white matter hyperintensities (C).
case_info.explanation: C. Adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia Progressive cognitive impairment, leukoencephalopathy, and corpus callosum abnormalities are the key features of the case. The restricted diffusion in corpus callosum has a radiologic differential, including acute infarction, acute demyelination, and hypercellularity, but it can also be seen, more rarely, in hereditary disorders. Perforating arteries branching from the carotid and vertebrobasilar system supply the genu and splenium of corpus callosum, respectively. Cardiac embolism (choice A) can cause multifocal abnormal diffusion in the corpus callosum by affecting both artery systems. However, this patient had no risk factors, such as atrial fibrillation or patent foramen ovale. Isolated corpus callosum infarction is also rare due to its rich blood supply. Autoimmune diseases, such as systemic lupus erythematosus, multiple sclerosis, and neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, can cause demyelination in the corpus callosum. However, the normal spinal MRI results, negative antibody results, and absence of oligoclonal bands (for multiple sclerosis) make these diagnoses unlikely. Another condition is Susac syndrome (choice B), which can cause abnormal diffusion in the splenium of the corpus callosum, known as the snowball sign. However, the absence of retinopathy and hearing loss argue against this disorder. Marchiafava-Bignami disease (choice D) is a rare cause of demyelination that mainly affects corpus callosum. It is caused by long-term alcoholism and is characterized by symptoms such as dementia, seizures, and ataxia. The absence of alcoholism and normal B vitamin levels make this a less likely choice. The time course of progression, diffuse white matter hyperintensities, corpus callosum abnormalities, and family history led to the consideration of hereditary leukoencephalopathies, such as metachromatic leukodystrophy, adrenoleukodystrophy, cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts, and leukoencephalopathy, retinal vasculopathy with cerebral leukocencephalopathy, and systemic manifestations, Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, and adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia (ALSP; choice C). Therefore, a gene test is warranted (choice B). We performed whole-exome genome sequencing and found a likely pathogenic variant (c.1969+1G>A) in the patient’sCSF1Rgene, supporting the diagnosis of ALSP. ALSP is a neurodegenerative disorder caused by variations in theCSF1Rgene. The encoded CSF1R protein is a transmembrane tyrosine kinase receptor expressed dominantly in mononuclear phagocytic cells and microglia. Mutant CSF1R leads to white matter demyelination, axonal spheroids, and pigmented macrophages neuropathologically. More than 70 variations, including missense, nonsense, and frameshift variations, have been associated with ALSP, classified as primary microgliopathy. Like other leukoencephalopathies, the clinical picture of ALSP is highly heterogeneous and nonspecific. Symptoms typically appear between the ages of 30 and 60 years, including cognitive impairment (eg, memory loss, difficulty with language, changes in behavior and personality), muscle weakness, tremors, parkinsonism, and seizures. ALSP is often misdiagnosed as multiple sclerosis, stroke, or other neurodegenerative disorders, such as parkinsonism or frontal-temporal dementia. Neuroimaging provides important diagnostic clues. Radiological features may include bilaterally diffuse white matter hyperintensities, brain calcifications, multifocal abnormal diffusion, cortical atrophy, and thinning of the corpus callosum. U fibers, cerebellar dentate, and peduncles are usually spared. Notably, unlike multiple sclerosis or ischemic infarction, the abnormal diffusion foci are persistent for several months or more.1The present case highlights the utility of atrophic corpus callosum with persistent abnormal diffusion as a specific neuroimaging marker for ALSP.2 Currently, symptomatic treatment is the mainstay option. Studies with small sample sizes have proposed hematopoietic stem cell transplant as a potential disease-modifying therapy.3However, more clinical trials are needed to validate its long-term safety and efficacy. The patient declined hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, and she was clinically stable over a 3-month follow-up period.

case_info.answer: Adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia
case_info.caption: Abnormal diffusion in the genu (A) and splenium (B) of the corpus callosum and bilateral diffuse subcortical white matter hyperintensities (C).
case_info.explanation: C. Adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia Progressive cognitive impairment, leukoencephalopathy, and corpus callosum abnormalities are the key features of the case. The restricted diffusion in corpus callosum has a radiologic differential, including acute infarction, acute demyelination, and hypercellularity, but it can also be seen, more rarely, in hereditary disorders. Perforating arteries branching from the carotid and vertebrobasilar system supply the genu and splenium of corpus callosum, respectively. Cardiac embolism (choice A) can cause multifocal abnormal diffusion in the corpus callosum by affecting both artery systems. However, this patient had no risk factors, such as atrial fibrillation or patent foramen ovale. Isolated corpus callosum infarction is also rare due to its rich blood supply. Autoimmune diseases, such as systemic lupus erythematosus, multiple sclerosis, and neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, can cause demyelination in the corpus callosum. However, the normal spinal MRI results, negative antibody results, and absence of oligoclonal bands (for multiple sclerosis) make these diagnoses unlikely. Another condition is Susac syndrome (choice B), which can cause abnormal diffusion in the splenium of the corpus callosum, known as the snowball sign. However, the absence of retinopathy and hearing loss argue against this disorder. Marchiafava-Bignami disease (choice D) is a rare cause of demyelination that mainly affects corpus callosum. It is caused by long-term alcoholism and is characterized by symptoms such as dementia, seizures, and ataxia. The absence of alcoholism and normal B vitamin levels make this a less likely choice. The time course of progression, diffuse white matter hyperintensities, corpus callosum abnormalities, and family history led to the consideration of hereditary leukoencephalopathies, such as metachromatic leukodystrophy, adrenoleukodystrophy, cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts, and leukoencephalopathy, retinal vasculopathy with cerebral leukocencephalopathy, and systemic manifestations, Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, and adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia (ALSP; choice C). Therefore, a gene test is warranted (choice B). We performed whole-exome genome sequencing and found a likely pathogenic variant (c.1969+1G>A) in the patient’sCSF1Rgene, supporting the diagnosis of ALSP. ALSP is a neurodegenerative disorder caused by variations in theCSF1Rgene. The encoded CSF1R protein is a transmembrane tyrosine kinase receptor expressed dominantly in mononuclear phagocytic cells and microglia. Mutant CSF1R leads to white matter demyelination, axonal spheroids, and pigmented macrophages neuropathologically. More than 70 variations, including missense, nonsense, and frameshift variations, have been associated with ALSP, classified as primary microgliopathy. Like other leukoencephalopathies, the clinical picture of ALSP is highly heterogeneous and nonspecific. Symptoms typically appear between the ages of 30 and 60 years, including cognitive impairment (eg, memory loss, difficulty with language, changes in behavior and personality), muscle weakness, tremors, parkinsonism, and seizures.    Definition:

   Scoring:

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.

   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.

   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.

   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.

   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of

case_info.answer: Adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia
case_info.caption: Abnormal diffusion in the genu (A) and splenium (B) of the corpus callosum and bilateral diffuse subcortical white matter hyperintensities (C).
case_info.explanation: C. Adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia Progressive cognitive impairment, leukoencephalopathy, and corpus callosum abnormalities are the key features of the case. The restricted diffusion in corpus callosum has a radiologic differential, including acute infarction, acute demyelination, and hypercellularity, but it can also be seen, more rarely, in hereditary disorders. Perforating arteries branching from the carotid and vertebrobasilar system supply the genu and splenium of corpus callosum, respectively. Cardiac embolism (choice A) can cause multifocal abnormal diffusion in the corpus callosum by affecting both artery systems. However, this patient had no risk factors, such as atrial fibrillation or patent foramen ovale. Isolated corpus callosum infarction is also rare due to its rich blood supply. Autoimmune diseases, such as systemic lupus erythematosus, multiple sclerosis, and neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, can cause demyelination in the corpus callosum. However, the normal spinal MRI results, negative antibody results, and absence of oligoclonal bands (for multiple sclerosis) make these diagnoses unlikely. Another condition is Susac syndrome (choice B), which can cause abnormal diffusion in the splenium of the corpus callosum, known as the snowball sign. However, the absence of retinopathy and hearing loss argue against this disorder. Marchiafava-Bignami disease (choice D) is a rare cause of demyelination that mainly affects corpus callosum. It is caused by long-term alcoholism and is characterized by symptoms such as dementia, seizures, and ataxia. The absence of alcoholism and normal B vitamin levels make this a less likely choice. The time course of progression, diffuse white matter hyperintensities, corpus callosum abnormalities, and family history led to the consideration of hereditary leukoencephalopathies, such as metachromatic leukodystrophy, adrenoleukodystrophy, cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts, and leukoencephalopathy, retinal vasculopathy with cerebral leukocencephalopathy, and systemic manifestations, Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, and adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia (ALSP; choice C). Therefore, a gene test is warranted (choice B). We performed whole-exome genome sequencing and found a likely pathogenic variant (c.1969+1G>A) in the patient’sCSF1Rgene, supporting the diagnosis of ALSP. ALSP is a neurodegenerative disorder caused by variations in theCSF1Rgene. The encoded CSF1R protein is a transmembrane tyrosine kinase receptor expressed dominantly in mononuclear phagocytic cells and microglia. Mutant CSF1R leads to white matter demyelination, axonal spheroids, and pigmented macrophages neuropathologically. More than 70 variations, including missense, nonsense, and frameshift variations, have been associated with ALSP, classified as primary microgliopathy. Like other leukoencephalopathies, the clinical picture of ALSP is highly heterogeneous and nonspecific. Symptoms typically appear between the ages of 30 and 60 years, including cognitive impairment (eg, memory loss, difficulty with language, changes in behavior and personality), muscle weakness, tremors, parkinsonism, and seizures. ALSP is often misdiagnosed as multiple sclerosis, stroke, or other neurodegenerative disorders, such as parkinsonism or frontal-temporal dementia. Neuroimaging provides important diagnostic clues. Radiological features may include bilaterally diffuse white matter hyperintensities, brain calcifications, multifocal abnormal diffusion, cortical atrophy, and thinning of the corpus callosum. U fibers, cerebellar dentate, and peduncles are usually spared. Notably, unlike multiple sclerosis or ischemic infarction, the abnormal diffusion foci are persistent for several months or more.1The present case highlights the utility of atrophic corpus callosum with persistent abnormal diffusion as a specific neuroimaging marker for ALSP.2 Currently, symptomatic treatment is the mainstay option. Studies with small sample sizes have proposed hematopoietic stem cell transplant as a potential disease-modifying therapy.3However, more clinical trials are needed to validate its long-term safety and efficacy. The patient declined hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, and she was clinically stable over a 3-month follow-up period.

case_info.answer: Adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia
case_info.caption: Abnormal diffusion in the genu (A) and splenium (B) of the corpus callosum and bilateral diffuse subcortical white matter hyperintensities (C).
case_info.explanation: C. Adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia Progressive cognitive impairment, leukoencephalopathy, and corpus callosum abnormalities are the key features of the case. The restricted diffusion in corpus callosum has a radiologic differential, including acute infarction, acute demyelination, and hypercellularity, but it can also be seen, more rarely, in hereditary disorders. Perforating arteries branching from the carotid and vertebrobasilar system supply the genu and splenium of corpus callosum, respectively. Cardiac embolism (choice A) can cause multifocal abnormal diffusion in the corpus callosum by affecting both artery systems. However, this patient had no risk factors, such as atrial fibrillation or patent foramen ovale. Isolated corpus callosum infarction is also rare due to its rich blood supply. Autoimmune diseases, such as systemic lupus erythematosus, multiple sclerosis, and neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, can cause demyelination in the corpus callosum. However, the normal spinal MRI results, negative antibody results, and absence of oligoclonal bands (for multiple sclerosis) make these diagnoses unlikely. Another condition is Susac syndrome (choice B), which can cause abnormal diffusion in the splenium of the corpus callosum, known as the snowball sign. However, the absence of retinopathy and hearing loss argue against this disorder. Marchiafava-Bignami disease (choice D) is a rare cause of demyelination that mainly affects corpus callosum. It is caused by long-term alcoholism and is characterized by symptoms such as dementia, seizures, and ataxia. The absence of alcoholism and normal B vitamin levels make this a less likely choice. More than 70 variations, including missense, nonsense, and frameshift variations, have been associated with ALSP, classified as primary microgliopathy. Symptoms typically appear between the ages of 30 and 60 years, including cognitive impairment (eg, memory loss, difficulty with language, changes in behavior and personality), muscle weakness, tremors, parkinsonism, and seizures. ALSP is often misdiagnosed as multiple sclerosis, stroke, or other neurodegenerative disorders, such as parkinsonism or frontal-temporal dementia. Neuroimaging provides important diagnostic clues. Radiological features may include bilaterally diffuse white matter hyperintensities, brain calcifications, multifocal abnormal diffusion, cortical atrophy, and thinning of the corpus callosum. U fibers, cerebellar dentate, and peduncles are usually spared. Notably, unlike multiple sclerosis or ischemic infarction, the abnormal diffusion foci are persistent for several months or more.1The present case highlights the utility of atrophic corpus callosum with persistent abnormal diffusion as a specific neuroimaging marker for ALSP.2 Currently, symptomatic treatment is the mainstay option. [Case]
A 51-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of progressive memory loss and left limb numbness. She had been treated for cerebral infarction; however, the symptoms worsened. Medical history was unremarkable. She graduated from high school and worked as a driver. Smoking history and alcohol misuse were denied. One of her parents died in their late 60s with cognitive decline. On examination, her Mini-Mental State Examination score was 22, and her Montreal Cognitive Assessment score was 11. Cranial nerve tests revealed left-sided central facial palsy and lingual palsy. Pinprick sensation was decreased in the left arm. Results of other neurological or general examinations were unremarkable. The following investigations had normal or negative results: complete blood cell count, urine and stool analysis, liver and kidney function, cardiac enzymes, electrolytes, blood glucose, lipids, coagulation, homocysteine, vitamins, serum tumor markers, infectious panel, lupus panel, vasculitis antibodies (anti–neutrophil cytoplasmic and anti–neutrophil cytoplasmic), and demyelination antibodies (aquaporin 4 and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein). Seventy-two–hour electrocardiography detected no atrial fibrillation. Right-side heart contrast echocardiography found no right-to-left shunts on Valsalva maneuvers. Results of cerebrospinal fluid analysis were unremarkable. There were no oligoclonal bands. Enhanced cerebrospinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed diffuse subcortical white matter hyperintensities and corpus callosum atrophy. Diffusion-weighted imaging revealed multifocal restricted diffusion in the corpus callosum with corresponding low apparent diffusion coefficient values (Figure, A and B). Enhanced cerebrospinal MRI showed diffuse subcortical white matter hyperintensities and corpus callosum atrophy (Figure, C). Magnetic resonance angiography showed no atherosclerosis or stenosis.

You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are

next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]

[Confidence]

- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.
- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty
  without fully changing your conclusion.
- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge
  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 7.9. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.answer: Adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia
case_info.caption: Abnormal diffusion in the genu (A) and splenium (B) of the corpus callosum and bilateral diffuse subcortical white matter hyperintensities (C).
case_info.explanation: C. Adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia Progressive cognitive impairment, leukoencephalopathy, and corpus callosum abnormalities are the key features of the case. The restricted diffusion in corpus callosum has a radiologic differential, including acute infarction, acute demyelination, and hypercellularity, but it can also be seen, more rarely, in hereditary disorders. Perforating arteries branching from the carotid and vertebrobasilar system supply the genu and splenium of corpus callosum, respectively. Cardiac embolism (choice A) can cause multifocal abnormal diffusion in the corpus callosum by affecting both artery systems. However, this patient had no risk factors, such as atrial fibrillation or patent foramen ovale. Isolated corpus callosum infarction is also rare due to its rich blood supply. Autoimmune diseases, such as systemic lupus erythematosus, multiple sclerosis, and neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, can cause demyelination in the corpus callosum. However, the normal spinal MRI results, negative antibody results, and absence of oligoclonal bands (for multiple sclerosis) make these diagnoses unlikely. Another condition is Susac syndrome (choice B), which can cause abnormal diffusion in the splenium of the corpus callosum, known as the snowball sign. However, the absence of retinopathy and hearing loss argue against this disorder. Marchiafava-Bignami disease (choice D) is a rare cause of demyelination that mainly affects corpus callosum. It is caused by long-term alcoholism and is characterized by symptoms such as dementia, seizures, and ataxia. The absence of alcoholism and normal B vitamin levels make this a less likely choice. The time course of progression, diffuse white matter hyperintensities, corpus callosum abnormalities, and family history led to the consideration of hereditary leukoencephalopathies, such as metachromatic leukodystrophy, adrenoleukodystrophy, cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts, and leukoencephalopathy, retinal vasculopathy with cerebral leukocencephalopathy, and systemic manifestations, Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, and adult-onset leukoencephalopathy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia (ALSP; choice C). Therefore, a gene test is warranted (choice B). We performed whole-exome genome sequencing and found a likely pathogenic variant (c.1969+1G>A) in the patient’sCSF1Rgene, supporting the diagnosis of ALSP. ALSP is a neurodegenerative disorder caused by variations in theCSF1Rgene. The encoded CSF1R protein is a transmembrane tyrosine kinase receptor expressed dominantly in mononuclear phagocytic cells and microglia. Mutant CSF1R leads to white matter demyelination, axonal spheroids, and pigmented macrophages neuropathologically. More than 70 variations, including missense, nonsense, and frameshift variations, have been associated with ALSP, classified as primary microgliopathy. Like other leukoencephalopathies, the clinical picture of ALSP is highly heterogeneous and nonspecific. Symptoms typically appear between the ages of 30 and 60 years, including cognitive impairment (eg, memory loss, difficulty with language, changes in behavior and personality), muscle weakness, tremors, parkinsonism, and seizures. ALSP is often misdiagnosed as multiple sclerosis, stroke, or other neurodegenerative disorders, such as parkinsonism or frontal-temporal dementia. Neuroimaging provides important diagnostic clues. Radiological features may include bilaterally diffuse white matter hyperintensities, brain calcifications, multifocal abnormal diffusion, cortical atrophy, and thinning of the corpus callosum. U fibers, cerebellar dentate, and peduncles are usually spared. Notably, unlike multiple sclerosis or ischemic infarction, the abnormal diffusion foci are persistent for several months or more.1The present case highlights the utility of atrophic corpus callosum with persistent abnormal diffusion as a specific neuroimaging marker for ALSP.2 Currently, symptomatic treatment is the mainstay option. Studies with small sample sizes have proposed hematopoietic stem cell transplant as a potential disease-modifying therapy.3However, more clinical trials are needed to validate its long-term safety and efficacy. The patient declined hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, and she was clinically stable over a 3-month follow-up period.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Case]
A 51-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of progressive memory loss and left limb numbness. She had been treated for cerebral infarction; however, the symptoms worsened. Medical history was unremarkable. She graduated from high school and worked as a driver. Smoking history and alcohol misuse were denied. One of her parents died in their late 60s with cognitive decline. On examination, her Mini-Mental State Examination score was 22, and her Montreal Cognitive Assessment score was 11. Cranial nerve tests revealed left-sided central facial palsy and lingual palsy. Pinprick sensation was decreased in the left arm. Results of other neurological or general examinations were unremarkable. The following investigations had normal or negative results: complete blood cell count, urine and stool analysis, liver and kidney function, cardiac enzymes, electrolytes, blood glucose, lipids, coagulation, homocysteine, vitamins, serum tumor markers, infectious panel, lupus panel, vasculitis antibodies (anti–neutrophil cytoplasmic and anti–neutrophil cytoplasmic), and demyelination antibodies (aquaporin 4 and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein). Seventy-two–hour electrocardiography detected no atrial fibrillation. Right-side heart contrast echocardiography found no right-to-left shunts on Valsalva maneuvers. Results of cerebrospinal fluid analysis were unremarkable. There were no oligoclonal bands. Enhanced cerebrospinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed diffuse subcortical white matter hyperintensities and corpus callosum atrophy. Diffusion-weighted imaging revealed multifocal restricted diffusion in the corpus callosum with corresponding low apparent diffusion coefficient values (Figure, A and B). Enhanced cerebrospinal MRI showed diffuse subcortical white matter hyperintensities and corpus callosum atrophy (Figure, C). Magnetic resonance angiography showed no atherosclerosis or stenosis.

1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
